tweets.text: If you've ever wondered why smart TVs are so cheap, this is why. @log4j rooted his Samsung and found an always-on hot mic, automatic content recognition, geolocation, network mapping, ad targeting and user profiling, shared with Samsung's "400 partners". A lot of it can be blocked in <15 min, wrote a basic guide below. What your TV is doing The main culprit is ACR (automatic content recognition). Your TV screenshots what's on screen, fingerprints it, and sends it home to build your ad profile. Samsung does it every 500ms, LG every 10ms [1]. What is insane: it happens on connected devices too. Plug in your laptop, your console, your work machine, and your TV can fingerprint that via HDMI [1]. He also found that if your Samsung doesn't have a mic, it'll look for one from a connected soundbar or bluetooth device. nitterk.kareem.one/log4j/status/211376224… It's on by default, and you likely agreed to it on the setup screen you clicked through in 10 seconds. Step 1: Turn off ACR Samsung: Terms & Privacy → Viewing Information Services LG: Live Plus Vizio: Viewing Data Roku: "Use info from TV inputs" Sony/Google TV: Samba Interactive TV Menus vary by model, but those are the names to look for. While you're in there, opt out of interest-based ads, reset your advertising ID, decline every optional privacy agreement, turn off voice recognition, and delete apps you never open. Step 2: Give smart devices their own network Put the TV, cameras, speakers and vacuum on your router's guest/IoT network. The logic is simple: these devices rarely get patched. If one gets compromised (getting drastically more frequent with AI), it shouldn't be able to see your other devices or home network. Step 3: Block trackers for the whole house with DNS-level filtering NextDNS (cloud-based) is easy and has a solid free plan. Pi-hole is a little bit more work if you prefer self hosting. For simplicity we'll focus on the former. 1. Sign up at nextdns.io (free tier is plenty) 2. Privacy tab: add a blocklist (OISD is a good bet) and turn on Native Tracking Protection for Samsung, LG, Roku, Amazon (see attached image) 3. Setup tab: copy your endpoint 4. Paste it into your router's DNS settings as DNS-over-HTTPS/TLS (or use the IPs + "Link IP" if your router only does plain DNS) 5. Bonus: block outbound port 53 except to your router. Some devices hardcode their own DNS to get around you Then open the NextDNS logs and watch how often your TV phones home. It's eye-opening. If an app or update breaks, find the domain in the logs and allowlist it. Why they do this TV prices are down 97% since 2000 [2]. Most of that is better manufacturing and brutal competition. But once margins on the hardware hit zero, the cost moved to you. In Q3 2024, Vizio lost $6.7M selling TVs and made $115.8M in gross profit from ads and viewing data [3]. They've said on earnings calls that they keep TV prices low to grow the audience they sell to advertisers. Walmart bought them in 2024. This isn't a conspiracy theory either. Vizio paid $2.2M to the FTC in 2017 for tracking 11 million TVs without consent. Last December, Texas sued Samsung, LG, Sony, Hisense and TCL over ACR. Samsung and LG have since agreed to stop collecting that data without explicit consent [4]. TL;DR 1. ACR off 2. Ads + voice off 3. Smart devices on their own network 4. NextDNS filtering on the router Sources: [1] ACR study: arxiv.org/abs/2409.06203 [2] Cost of US consumer goods: aei.org/economics/chart-of-t… [3] Vizio Q3 2024: sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/… [4] Texas v. Dusting off this tweet from April because this gap in shared understanding of LLM capability is *widening*. It's now less "two groups of people speaking past each other" and more a sharp funnel. - Napkin math somewhere around 6B people (~75% of the population) have barely come in contact with LLMs at all. - Around 1-2B (~20%) are casual and infrequent users of free-tier ChatGPT-like products. This group sees derpy chatbots and treats them a bit like a better Google search, a writing aid, or etc. Maybe an agent tries to book you a flight. I have non-tech friends who (reasonably, imo) say they have not much use for it at all. Even many professionals outside of math&code are in this tier. For example, execs and many other functions spend a lot of their time talking to other people, so while they understand what is happening intellectually, it is still second-hand and a bit abstract. - Now we get to professional use of frontier-grade LLMs in math&code. Somewhere around 20M people (0.2%) see first-hand that large, complex projects that used to take them weeks/months can now be completed by agents with a prompt. Building apps, copying apps, translating apps, decompiling apps from binaries... This has all happened very quickly and recently - less than 1 year ago, I was writing code manually by hand, typing memorized computer code commands into a code editor character by character, occasionally pressing Tab to autocomplete a little chunk of code. - And finally we get to the ~5,000 people (~0.00006%) with access to frontier-grade systems internally. The external world has seen the preview. It looks like swarms of thousands of agents collaborating over weeks on software mega projects: minting zero days, running cyber attacks and defenses at machine speeds, discovering new science, advancing the frontier of mathematics. Things that would have taken top professionals in the industry years of work. Meanwhile, human review and comprehension are starting to fall behind. For example, people are still involved in the "archeology" of the OpenAI-HF incident from many months ago. Mathematicians may be poring over the 722 manuscripts on frontier mathematics for a while. The funnel is driven by a combination of factors: 1. The impact scales with ambition, problem size, and horizon. A question with a paragraph answer barely stresses the system. You need a reservoir of big, difficult problems that you really care about. This aspect drives the consumer / professional dimension of the funnel. 2. The jaggedness of the system (which I have written about a lot separately). Capability peaks in domains that are digital, verifiable and economically valuable. This is because LLM capability emerges from reinforcement learning on verifiable rewards on a curated environment mixture driven by revenue potential. This aspect primarily drives the area (e.g. math&code) dimension of the funnel. 3. Access. Free-tier, paid-tier, internal. So this is the weirdness of the moment. The general public has mostly not interacted with these systems. When they have, it looks like a derpy chatbot. The majority of professionals still see only a modest uplift. And a small sliver of professionals are experiencing the vertigo of the curve going vertical. And it is all happening at the same time. Andrej Karpathy (@karpathy) Judging by my tl there is a growing gap in understanding of AI capability. The first issue I think is around recency and tier of use. I think a lot of people tried the free tier of ChatGPT somewhere last year and allowed it to inform their views on AI a little too much. This is a group of reactions laughing at various quirks of the models, hallucinations, etc. Yes I also saw the viral videos of OpenAI's Advanced Voice mode fumbling simple queries like "should I drive or walk to the carwash". The thing is that these free and old/deprecated models don't reflect the capability in the latest round of state of the art agentic models of this year, especially OpenAI Codex and Claude Code. But that brings me to the second issue. Even if people paid $200/month to use the state of the art models, a lot of the capabilities are relatively "peaky" in highly technical areas. Typical queries around search, writing, advice, etc. are *not* the domain that has made the most noticeable and dramatic strides in capability. Partly, this is due to the technical details of reinforcement learning and its use of verifiable rewards. But partly, it's also because these use cases are not sufficiently prioritized by the companies in their hillclimbing because they don't lead to as much $$$ value. The goldmines are elsewhere, and the focus comes along. So that brings me to the second group of people, who *both* 1) pay for and use the state of the art frontier agentic models (OpenAI Codex / Claude Code) and 2) do so professionally in technical domains like programming, math and research. This group of people is subject to the highest amount of "AI Psychosis" because the recent improvements in these domains as of this year have been nothing short of staggering. When you hand a computer terminal to one of these models, you can now watch them melt programming problems that you'd normally expect to take days/weeks of work. It's this second group of people that assigns a much greater gravity to the capabilities, their slope, and various cyber-related repercussions. TLDR the people in these two groups are speaking past each other. It really is simultaneously the case that OpenAI's free and I think slightly orphaned (?) "Advanced Voice Mode" will fumble the dumbest questions in your Instagram's reels and *at the same time*, OpenAI's highest-tier and paid Codex model will go off for 1 hour to coherently restructure an entire code base, or find and exploit vulnerabilities in computer systems. This part really works and has made dramatic strides because 2 properties: 1) these domains offer explicit reward functions that are verifiable meaning they are easily amenable to reinforcement learning training (e.g. unit tests passed yes or no, in contrast to writing, which is much harder to explicitly judge), but also 2) they are a lot more valuable in b2b settings, meaning that the biggest fraction of the team is focused on improving them. So here we are. — https://nitter.kareem.one/karpathy/status/2042334451611693415#m

We'll be spending a lot more time trying to understand the outputs of language models. A few thoughts, tips & tricks: Writing. Something I've had success with: Ask your LLM to explain something in ASD-STE100, it's a controlled language specification originally developed for aerospace maintenance documentation. LLMs well-versed in this language and it comes with heavy constraints on clean writing style that I often find a lot more readable. Sometimes I've tried to soften it a bit e.g. ask for "80% of the way to ASD-STE100" because the spec is quite stringent. But even better: Diagrams / images. Instead of writing, ask your LLM to create a diagram. These can be a lot easier to process, parse, and understand. But even better: Web pages. Ask for output "in HTML" to get a beautiful, interactive webpage. LLMs are getting really good at frontend and can create beautiful experiences, animations, etc. But even better: Explainer videos. The output format I am most bullish on is fully custom / bespoke explainer videos generated on any arbitrary topic. Experiment with things like "Create a 3b1b style video explainer on X. Use my ElevenLabs API key for audio narration". (you'd need an API key for the latter or you can ask your LLM to find you decent free alternatives that use your local compute). This is actually starting to work! In summary: - As LLMs get better, they will do more and more of the legwork autonomously, and a lot more of our work will rise up the abstractions into oversight and understanding. - Luckily, LLMs can help here too because as intelligence and code are increasingly abundant, you can ask for large, custom, discardable software artifacts (e.g. web apps, video explainers) that would have never made sense to create before. Push the boundaries here and you'll be surprised.

Yann LeCun has changed the game for robotics. Research he co-authored tackles a problem inside AI world models: their internal representations can make planning harder than it needs to be. A world model predicts what happens after an action. But even useful visual features can form curved paths in its internal “map,” making distance to a goal misleading. The researchers introduced Temporal Straightening. During training, it encourages those internal paths to become straighter, so the planner gets a more useful measure of progress. The results: More stable gradient-based planning Higher success rates across tested goal-reaching tasks Code available for others to explore The approach changes how the model represents movement, rather than rewriting every RL algorithm to work in curved space. For robotics, that’s a useful direction: build world models whose internal maps help an agent choose its next move.

processed.summary: Cette journée offre un panorama riche pour les passionnés d'IA. Nous avons vu des conseils pratiques pour protéger notre vie privée face aux technologies embarquées, ainsi que des méthodes innovantes pour mieux interagir avec les IA. La communauté est en effervescence avec le partage de modèles 3D et de données d'entraînement. Mais surtout, de grandes réflexions ont émergé sur le fossé de compréhension des capacités de l'IA et sur la manière dont les entreprises pourraient se transformer grâce aux agents autonomes.

glossaire.definition: Un programme informatique très puissant capable de comprendre, générer du texte, traduire, écrire et répondre à des questions de manière informative.
Technologie permettant à un téléviseur intelligent de reconnaître le contenu que vous regardez (émissions, publicités) pour collecter des données sur vos habitudes.
Un système qui utilise un LLM pour accomplir des tâches complexes de manière autonome, en planifiant des étapes, en exécutant des actions et en s'adaptant à l'environnement.
En IA, c'est un système qui permet à une machine de prédire les conséquences de ses actions dans un environnement donné, comme un robot qui imagine l'effet d'un mouvement.

glossaire.terme: Open source / Modèle à poids ouverts
glossaire.definition: Désigne un logiciel ou un modèle d'IA dont le code ou les paramètres internes sont rendus publics, permettant à quiconque de les utiliser, les étudier et les améliorer librement.
Une méthode qui empêche les appareils de votre réseau d'accéder à certains sites web ou serveurs connus pour collecter des données ou afficher des publicités indésirables.
Un format de fichier universel développé par Pixar pour décrire des scènes 3D complexes, facilitant l'échange de données entre différents logiciels de création et de simulation.

category_summaries.actu: Aujourd'hui, les annonces mettent en lumière des recherches importantes en robotique visant à améliorer la planification des agents, la sortie du premier 'Modèle du Monde d'Ingénierie' et de nouvelles politiques chinoises sur l'IA et l'emploi. Anthropic a également publié un rapport crucial sur la manière dont son modèle Claude a été détourné et les mesures prises pour y remédier.
category_summaries.tips: Les conseils du jour sont essentiels pour tout débutant : apprenez à protéger votre vie privée face aux fonctionnalités de suivi des téléviseurs connectés en quelques étapes simples. Découvrez aussi comment optimiser vos interactions avec les IA en leur demandant des formats de sortie plus riches et variés, comme des diagrammes, des pages web interactives ou même des vidéos explicatives.
category_summaries.idees: De nombreuses réflexions ont animé la journée, notamment sur le fossé grandissant dans la compréhension des capacités réelles de l'IA, allant du chatbot simple aux systèmes de pointe. Des discussions sur l'automatisation totale de l'ingénierie logicielle et les implications du 'doomerisme' en IA ont aussi été abordées. Enfin, la vision d'une 'entreprise auto-pilotée' par des agents IA a suscité un débat passionnant sur l'avenir du travail et des organisations.
category_summaries.outils: Côté outils, la communauté a été gâtée : une nouvelle méthode d'évaluation montre les capacités insoupçonnées des LLM à 'comprimer' des connaissances géographiques. Cohere a fait preuve de transparence en ouvrant les 'traces' de son modèle pour la reproduction de comportements inhabituels. De plus, Hugging Face est désormais un hub pour des milliers de modèles 3D open source et a lancé le support du format OpenUSD, facilitant la création et la simulation.

highlights.text_fr:
Andrej Karpathy met en lumière un fossé grandissant dans la compréhension des capacités des modèles de langage (LLM). Il décrit une sorte d'entonnoir :
    *   La grande majorité (75% de la population mondiale) n'a jamais ou à peine utilisé de LLM.
    *   Environ 20% sont des utilisateurs occasionnels de versions gratuites (comme ChatGPT), percevant les chatbots comme des outils d'aide à la recherche ou à l'écriture, parfois "bizarres".
    *   Puis, 0,2% (20 millions de personnes) sont des professionnels utilisant des LLM de pointe en mathématiques et programmation. Ils constatent que des projets complexes qui prenaient des semaines peuvent désormais être accomplis par des "agents" avec une simple instruction.
    *   Enfin, une infime élite (5000 personnes, 0,00006%) a accès à des systèmes internes de très haut niveau, capables de réaliser en quelques semaines des méga-projets logiciels, des cyberattaques/défenses, ou des découvertes scientifiques, ce qui prendrait des années à des experts humains.
Ce fossé s'explique par l'ambition des projets, le fait que les LLM excellent dans les domaines numériques et vérifiables (comme le code), et l'accès différencié aux modèles (gratuit, payant, interne). Il conclut que l'on vit une période étrange où les perceptions de l'IA sont simultanément très différentes : du chatbot simple aux systèmes ultra-performants.
highlights.text_original: Dusting off this tweet from April because this gap in shared understanding of LLM capability is *widening*. It's now less "two groups of people speaking past each other" and more a sharp funnel. - Napkin math somewhere around 6B people (~75% of the population) have barely come in contact with LLMs at all. - Around 1-2B (~20%) are casual and infrequent users of free-tier ChatGPT-like products. This group sees derpy chatbots and treats them a bit like a better Google search, a writing aid, or etc. Maybe an agent tries to book you a flight. I have non-tech friends who (reasonably, imo) say they have not much use for it at all. Even many professionals outside of math&code are in this tier. For example, execs and many other functions spend a lot of their time talking to other people, so while they understand what is happening intellectually, it is still second-hand and a bit abstract. - Now we get to professional use of frontier-grade LLMs in math&code. Somewhere around 20M people (0.2%) see first-hand that large, complex projects that used to take them weeks/months can now be completed by agents with a prompt. Building apps, copying apps, translating apps, decompiling apps from binaries... This has all happened very quickly and recently - less than 1 year ago, I was writing code manually by hand, typing memorized computer code commands into a code editor character by character, occasionally pressing Tab to autocomplete a little chunk of code. - And finally we get to the ~5,000 people (~0.00006%) with access to frontier-grade systems internally. The external world has seen the preview. It looks like swarms of thousands of agents collaborating over weeks on software mega projects: minting zero days, running cyber attacks and defenses at machine speeds, discovering new science, advancing the frontier of mathematics. Things that would have taken top professionals in the industry years of work. Meanwhile, human review and comprehension are starting to fall behind. For example, people are still involved in the "archeology" of the OpenAI-HF incident from many months ago. Mathematicians may be poring over the 722 manuscripts on frontier mathematics for a while. The funnel is driven by a combination of factors: 1. The impact scales with ambition, problem size, and horizon. A question with a paragraph answer barely stresses the system. You need a reservoir of big, difficult problems that you really care about. This aspect drives the consumer / professional dimension of the funnel. 2. The jaggedness of the system (which I have written about a lot separately). Capability peaks in domains that are digital, verifiable and economically valuable. This is because LLM capability emerges from reinforcement learning on verifiable rewards on a curated environment mixture driven by revenue potential. This aspect primarily drives the area (e.g. math&code) dimension of the funnel. 3. Access. Free-tier, paid-tier, internal. So this is the weirdness of the moment. The general public has mostly not interacted with these systems. When they have, it looks like a derpy chatbot. The majority of professionals still see only a modest uplift. And a small sliver of professionals are experiencing the vertigo of the curve going vertical. And it is all happening at the same time. Andrej Karpathy (@karpathy) Judging by my tl there is a growing gap in understanding of AI capability. The first issue I think is around recency and tier of use. I think a lot of people tried the free tier of ChatGPT somewhere last year and allowed it to inform their views on AI a little too much. This is a group of reactions laughing at various quirks of the models, hallucinations, etc. Yes I also saw the viral videos of OpenAI's Advanced Voice mode fumbling simple queries like "should I drive or walk to the carwash". The thing is that these free and old/deprecated models don't reflect the capability in the latest round of state of the art agentic models of this year, especially OpenAI Codex and Claude Code. But that brings me to the second issue. Even if people paid $200/month to use the state of the art models, a lot of the capabilities are relatively "peaky" in highly technical areas. Typical queries around search, writing, advice, etc. are *not* the domain that has made the most noticeable and dramatic strides in capability. Partly, this is due to the technical details of reinforcement learning and its use of verifiable rewards. But partly, it's also because these use cases are not sufficiently prioritized by the companies in their hillclimbing because they don't lead to as much $$$ value. The goldmines are elsewhere, and the focus comes along. So that brings me to the second group of people, who *both* 1) pay for and use the state of the art frontier agentic models (OpenAI Codex / Claude Code) and 2) do so professionally in technical domains like programming, math and research. This group of people is subject to the highest amount of "AI Psychosis" because the recent improvements in these domains as of this year have been nothing short of staggering. When you hand a computer terminal to one of these models, you can now watch them melt programming problems that you'd normally expect to take days/weeks of work. It's this second group of people that assigns a much greater gravity to the capabilities, their slope, and various cyber-related repercussions. TLDR the people in these two groups are speaking past each other. It really is simultaneously the case that OpenAI's free and I think slightly orphaned (?) "Advanced Voice Mode" will fumble the dumbest questions in your Instagram's reels and *at the same time*, OpenAI's highest-tier and paid Codex model will go off for 1 hour to coherently restructure an entire code base, or find and exploit vulnerabilities in computer systems. This part really works and has made dramatic strides because 2 properties: 1) these domains offer explicit reward functions that are verifiable meaning they are easily amenable to reinforcement learning training (e.g. unit tests passed yes or no, in contrast to writing, which is much harder to explicitly judge), but also 2) they are a lot more valuable in b2b settings, meaning that the biggest fraction of the team is focused on improving them. Nous allons passer de plus en plus de temps à essayer de comprendre les sorties des modèles de langage. Voici quelques réflexions, astuces et conseils :
    *   **Écriture :** Andrej a eu du succès en demandant à son LLM d'expliquer quelque chose en utilisant la spécification "ASD-STE100", un langage contrôlé développé pour la documentation de maintenance aérospatiale, qui impose un style d'écriture très clair. Il suggère même de demander une version "80% ASD-STE100" pour adoucir les contraintes.
    *   **Diagrammes / images :** Au lieu d'un texte, demandez à votre LLM de créer un diagramme pour une meilleure compréhension.
    *   **Pages web :** Demandez une sortie "en HTML" pour obtenir une page web interactive et esthétique, les LLM devenant très performants en frontend.
    *   **Vidéos explicatives :** Le format qui l'enthousiasme le plus est la vidéo explicative personnalisée générée sur n'importe quel sujet. Il suggère d'expérimenter avec des requêtes comme "Crée une vidéo explicative sur X, style 3b1b. Utilise ma clé API ElevenLabs pour la narration audio".
En résumé, à mesure que les LLM s'améliorent, notre travail se déplacera vers la supervision et la compréhension, et les LLM peuvent nous aider en créant des artefacts logiciels sur mesure (applications web, vidéos) qui n'auraient jamais eu de sens à créer auparavant.
highlights.text_original: We'll be spending a lot more time trying to understand the outputs of language models. A few thoughts, tips & tricks: Writing. Something I've had success with: Ask your LLM to explain something in ASD-STE100, it's a controlled language specification originally developed for aerospace maintenance documentation. LLMs well-versed in this language and it comes with heavy constraints on clean writing style that I often find a lot more readable. Sometimes I've tried to soften it a bit e.g. ask for "80% of the way to ASD-STE100" because the spec is quite stringent. But even better: Diagrams / images. Instead of writing, ask your LLM to create a diagram. These can be a lot easier to process, parse, and understand. But even better: Web pages. Ask for output "in HTML" to get a beautiful, interactive webpage. LLMs are getting really good at frontend and can create beautiful experiences, animations, etc. But even better: Explainer videos. The output format I am most bullish on is fully custom / bespoke explainer videos generated on any arbitrary topic. Experiment with things like "Create a 3b1b style video explainer on X. Use my ElevenLabs API key for audio narration". (you'd need an API key for the latter or you can ask your LLM to find you decent free alternatives that use your local compute). This is actually starting to work! In summary: - As LLMs get better, they will do more and more of the legwork autonomously, and a lot more of our work will rise up the abstractions into oversight and understanding. - Luckily, LLMs can help here too because as intelligence and code are increasingly abundant, you can ask for large, custom, discardable software artifacts (e.g. web apps, video explainers) that would have never made sense to create before. Push the boundaries here and you'll be surprised.

actu.text_fr: Yann LeCun a révolutionné la robotique grâce à une recherche dont il est co-auteur. Ce travail aborde un problème dans les "modèles du monde" des IA : leurs représentations internes peuvent rendre la planification plus difficile qu'elle ne devrait l'être. Un modèle du monde prédit ce qui se passe après une action. Mais même des caractéristiques visuelles utiles peuvent créer des chemins "courbes" dans sa "carte" interne, faussant la distance à un objectif. Les chercheurs ont introduit le "Temporal Straightening", qui, pendant l'entraînement, encourage ces chemins internes à devenir plus "droits", offrant ainsi au planificateur une mesure de progrès plus utile. Les résultats montrent une planification basée sur le gradient plus stable et des taux de réussite plus élevés pour les tâches d'atteinte d'objectifs testées. Le code est disponible pour exploration. Cette approche modifie la manière dont le modèle représente le mouvement, plutôt que de réécrire chaque algorithme d'apprentissage par renforcement (RL). C'est une direction prometteuse pour la robotique : créer des modèles du monde dont les cartes internes aident un agent à choisir sa prochaine action.
actu.text_original: Yann LeCun has changed the game for robotics. Research he co-authored tackles a problem inside AI world models: their internal representations can make planning harder than it needs to be. A world model predicts what happens after an action. But even useful visual features can form curved paths in its internal “map,” making distance to a goal misleading. The researchers introduced Temporal Straightening. During training, it encourages those internal paths to become straighter, so the planner gets a more useful measure of progress. The results: More stable gradient-based planning Higher success rates across tested goal-reaching tasks Code available for others to explore The approach changes how the model represents movement, rather than rewriting every RL algorithm to work in curved space. For robotics, that’s a useful direction: build world models whose internal maps help an agent choose its next move.
actu.decryptage: Un "modèle du monde" en IA est un système qui permet à une machine de prédire les conséquences de ses actions dans un environnement donné, comme un robot qui imagine l'effet d'un mouvement. Le "Temporal Straightening" est une technique qui aide l'IA à mieux "visualiser" son parcours vers un objectif, en rendant sa représentation interne des mouvements plus directe et moins "tordue". L'apprentissage par renforcement (RL) est une méthode où une IA apprend à prendre des décisions en recevant des récompenses ou des pénalités pour ses actions.

A lot of it can be blocked in <15 min, wrote a basic guide below. What your TV is doing The main culprit is ACR (automatic content recognition). Your TV screenshots what's on screen, fingerprints it, and sends it home to build your ad profile. Samsung does it every 500ms, LG every 10ms [1]. What is insane: it happens on connected devices too. Plug in your laptop, your console, your work machine, and your TV can fingerprint that via HDMI [1]. While you're in there, opt out of interest-based ads, reset your advertising ID, decline every optional privacy agreement, turn off voice recognition, and delete apps you never open. Step 2: Give smart devices their own network Put the TV, cameras, speakers and vacuum on your router's guest/IoT network. The logic is simple: these devices rarely get patched. tips.text_fr:
Nous allons passer de plus en plus de temps à essayer de comprendre les sorties des modèles de langage. Voici quelques réflexions, astuces et conseils :
    *   **Écriture :** Andrej a eu du succès en demandant à son LLM d'expliquer quelque chose en utilisant la spécification "ASD-STE100", un langage contrôlé développé pour la documentation de maintenance aérospatiale, qui impose un style d'écriture très clair. Il suggère même de demander une version "80% ASD-STE100" pour adoucir les contraintes.
    *   **Diagrammes / images :** Au lieu d'un texte, demandez à votre LLM de créer un diagramme pour une meilleure compréhension.
    *   **Pages web :** Demandez une sortie "en HTML" pour obtenir une page web interactive et esthétique, les LLM devenant très performants en frontend.
    *   **Vidéos explicatives :** Le format qui l'enthousiasme le plus est la vidéo explicative personnalisée générée sur n'importe quel sujet. Il suggère d'expérimenter avec des requêtes comme "Crée une vidéo explicative sur X, style 3b1b. Utilise ma clé API ElevenLabs pour la narration audio".
En résumé, à mesure que les LLM s'améliorent, notre travail se déplacera vers la supervision et la compréhension, et les LLM peuvent nous aider en créant des artefacts logiciels sur mesure (applications web, vidéos) qui n'auraient jamais eu de sens à créer auparavant.
tips.text_original: We'll be spending a lot more time trying to understand the outputs of language models. A few thoughts, tips & tricks: Writing. Something I've had success with: Ask your LLM to explain something in ASD-STE100, it's a controlled language specification originally developed for aerospace maintenance documentation. LLMs well-versed in this language and it comes with heavy constraints on clean writing style that I often find a lot more readable. Sometimes I've tried to soften it a bit e.g. ask for "80% of the way to ASD-STE100" because the spec is quite stringent. But even better: Diagrams / images. Instead of writing, ask your LLM to create a diagram. These can be a lot easier to process, parse, and understand. But even better: Web pages. Ask for output "in HTML" to get a beautiful, interactive webpage. LLMs are getting really good at frontend and can create beautiful experiences, animations, etc. But even better: Explainer videos. The output format I am most bullish on is fully custom / bespoke explainer videos generated on any arbitrary topic. Experiment with things like "Create a 3b1b style video explainer on X. Use my ElevenLabs API key for audio narration". (you'd need an API key for the latter or you can ask your LLM to find you decent free alternatives that use your local compute). This is actually starting to work! In summary: - As LLMs get better, they will do more and more of the legwork autonomously, and a lot more of our work will rise up the abstractions into oversight and understanding. - Luckily, LLMs can help here too because as intelligence and code are increasingly abundant, you can ask for large, custom, discardable software artifacts (e.g. web apps, video explainers) that would have never made sense to create before. Push the boundaries here and you'll be surprised.
tips.decryptage: ASD-STE100 est une norme de langage clair et simplifié, initialement utilisée dans l'aéronautique pour éviter toute ambiguïté. Demander une sortie "en HTML" signifie demander au LLM de générer le code d'une page web, qui pourra ensuite être affichée dans un navigateur. Une "clé API" est une sorte de mot de passe qui permet à un programme (comme un LLM) d'utiliser les services d'une autre entreprise (comme ElevenLabs pour la génération audio). Le "frontend" désigne la partie visible et interactive d'une application ou d'un site web, celle avec laquelle l'utilisateur interagit directement.

idees.text_fr:
Andrej Karpathy met en lumière un fossé grandissant dans la compréhension des capacités des modèles de langage (LLM). Il décrit une sorte d'entonnoir :
    *   La grande majorité (75% de la population mondiale) n'a jamais ou à peine utilisé de LLM.
    *   Environ 20% sont des utilisateurs occasionnels de versions gratuites (comme ChatGPT), percevant les chatbots comme des outils d'aide à la recherche ou à l'écriture, parfois "bizarres".
    *   Puis, 0,2% (20 millions de personnes) sont des professionnels utilisant des LLM de pointe en mathématiques et programmation. Ils constatent que des projets complexes qui prenaient des semaines peuvent désormais être accomplis par des "agents" avec une simple instruction.
    *   Enfin, une infime élite (5000 personnes, 0,00006%) a accès à des systèmes internes de très haut niveau, capables de réaliser en quelques semaines des méga-projets logiciels, des cyberattaques/défenses, ou des découvertes scientifiques, ce qui prendrait des années à des experts humains.
Ce fossé s'explique par l'ambition des projets, le fait que les LLM excellent dans les domaines numériques et vérifiables (comme le code), et l'accès différencié aux modèles (gratuit, payant, interne). Il conclut que l'on vit une période étrange où les perceptions de l'IA sont simultanément très différentes : du chatbot simple aux systèmes ultra-performants.
idees.text_original: Dusting off this tweet from April because this gap in shared understanding of LLM capability is *widening*. It's now less "two groups of people speaking past each other" and more a sharp funnel. - Napkin math somewhere around 6B people (~75% of the population) have barely come in contact with LLMs at all. - Around 1-2B (~20%) are casual and infrequent users of free-tier ChatGPT-like products. This group sees derpy chatbots and treats them a bit like a better Google search, a writing aid, or etc. Maybe an agent tries to book you a flight. I have non-tech friends who (reasonably, imo) say they have not much use for it at all. Even many professionals outside of math&code are in this tier. For example, execs and many other functions spend a lot of their time talking to other people, so while they understand what is happening intellectually, it is still second-hand and a bit abstract. - Now we get to professional use of frontier-grade LLMs in math&code. Somewhere around 20M people (0.2%) see first-hand that large, complex projects that used to take them weeks/months can now be completed by agents with a prompt. Building apps, copying apps, translating apps, decompiling apps from binaries... This has all happened very quickly and recently - less than 1 year ago, I was writing code manually by hand, typing memorized computer code commands into a code editor character by character, occasionally pressing Tab to autocomplete a little chunk of code. - And finally we get to the ~5,000 people (~0.00006%) with access to frontier-grade systems internally. The external world has seen the preview. It looks like swarms of thousands of agents collaborating over weeks on software mega projects: minting zero days, running cyber attacks and defenses at machine speeds, discovering new science, advancing the frontier of mathematics. Things that would have taken top professionals in the industry years of work. Meanwhile, human review and comprehension are starting to fall behind. For example, people are still involved in the "archeology" of the OpenAI-HF incident from many months ago. Mathematicians may be poring over the 722 manuscripts on frontier mathematics for a while. The funnel is driven by a combination of factors: 1. The impact scales with ambition, problem size, and horizon. A question with a paragraph answer barely stresses the system. You need a reservoir of big, difficult problems that you really care about. This aspect drives the consumer / professional dimension of the funnel. 2. The jaggedness of the system (which I have written about a lot separately). Capability peaks in domains that are digital, verifiable and economically valuable. This is because LLM capability emerges from reinforcement learning on verifiable rewards on a curated environment mixture driven by revenue potential. This aspect primarily drives the area (e.g. math&code) dimension of the funnel. 3. Access. Free-tier, paid-tier, internal. So this is the weirdness of the moment. The general public has mostly not interacted with these systems. When they have, it looks like a derpy chatbot. The majority of professionals still see only a modest uplift. And a small sliver of professionals are experiencing the vertigo of the curve going vertical. And it is all happening at the same time. Andrej Karpathy (@karpathy) Judging by my tl there is a growing gap in understanding of AI capability. The first issue I think is around recency and tier of use. I think a lot of people tried the free tier of ChatGPT somewhere last year and allowed it to inform their views on AI a little too much. This is a group of reactions laughing at various quirks of the models, hallucinations, etc. Yes I also saw the viral videos of OpenAI's Advanced Voice mode fumbling simple queries like "should I drive or walk to the carwash". The thing is that these free and old/deprecated models don't reflect the capability in the latest round of state of the art agentic models of this year, especially OpenAI Codex and Claude Code. But that brings me to the second issue. Even if people paid $200/month to use the state of the art models, a lot of the capabilities are relatively "peaky" in highly technical areas. Typical queries around search, writing, advice, etc. are *not* the domain that has made the most noticeable and dramatic strides in capability. Partly, this is due to the technical details of reinforcement learning and its use of verifiable rewards. But partly, it's also because these use cases are not sufficiently prioritized by the companies in their hillclimbing because they don't lead to as much $$$ value. The goldmines are elsewhere, and the focus comes along. So that brings me to the second group of people, who *both* 1) pay for and use the state of the art frontier agentic models (OpenAI Codex / Claude Code) and 2) do so professionally in technical domains like programming, math and research. This group of people is subject to the highest amount of "AI Psychosis" because the recent improvements in these domains as of this year have been nothing short of staggering. When you hand a computer terminal to one of these models, you can now watch them melt programming problems that you'd normally expect to take days/weeks of work. It's this second group of people that assigns a much greater gravity to the capabilities, their slope, and various cyber-related repercussions. TLDR the people in these two groups are speaking past each other. It really is simultaneously the case that OpenAI's free and I think slightly orphaned (?) "Advanced Voice Mode" will fumble the dumbest questions in your Instagram's reels and *at the same time*, OpenAI's highest-tier and paid Codex model will go off for 1 hour to coherently restructure an entire code base, or find and exploit vulnerabilities in computer systems. This part really works and has made dramatic strides because 2 properties: 1) these domains offer explicit reward functions that are verifiable meaning they are easily amenable to reinforcement learning training (e.g. unit tests passed yes or no, in contrast to writing, which is much harder to explicitly judge), but also 2) they are a lot more valuable in b2b settings, meaning that the biggest fraction of the team is focused on improving them. So here we are. — https://nitter.kareem.one/karpathy/status/2042334451611693415#m
idees.decryptage: Un "LLM" (Large Language Model) est un programme informatique très puissant, capable de comprendre et de générer du texte, de traduire des langues, d'écrire différents types de contenu créatif, et de répondre à vos questions de manière informative. Les "agents" IA sont des systèmes qui utilisent un LLM pour accomplir des tâches complexes de manière autonome, en planifiant des étapes, en exécutant des actions et en s'adaptant. Les "modèles de pointe" désignent les versions les plus avancées et performantes des LLM disponibles.

idees.text_fr: Un nouvel essai du magazine UnHerd aborde les aspects politiques autoritaires du "doomerisme" en IA. Il explique comment des expériences de pensée philosophiques se sont transformées en propositions de surveillance massive des chercheurs.
idees.text_original: This new UnHerd magazine essay is about the authoritarian politics of AI doomerism. It explains how it turned philosophical thought experiments into proposals for mass surveillance of researchers.
idees.decryptage: Le "doomerisme en IA" fait référence à une vision pessimiste et alarmiste de l'intelligence artificielle, où l'on craint que l'IA ne conduise à des scénarios catastrophes pour l'humanité, parfois jusqu'à proposer des mesures de contrôle très strictes.

L' "apprentissage symbolique" est une approche de l'IA qui se concentre sur l'utilisation de symboles et de règles logiques, plutôt que de réseaux neuronaux, pour traiter l'information, de manière plus similaire à la pensée humaine.

idees.text_fr:
Quelques observations sur l'automatisation "totale" de l'ingénierie logicielle :
    1.  Il y a plus d'ingénieurs logiciels aujourd'hui qu'en 2025, et la demande ne cesse de croître.
    2.  Les ingénieurs logiciels n'ont jamais travaillé aussi dur.
    3.  Ils n'écrivent plus beaucoup de code ; les "agents" s'occupent d'environ 100% du code.
    4.  Pourtant, le résultat financier des entreprises qui emploient ces ingénieurs et ces agents ne bouge généralement pas suite à l'adoption de l'IA.
C'est pourquoi il faut penser en termes de systèmes : automatiser un aspect d'un système crée ses propres frictions et déplace les goulots d'étranglement ailleurs.
idees.text_original: Some observations about the "total" automation of software engineering: 1. There are more software engineers now than in 2025, and demand is growing. 2. Software engineers have never worked harder than they do now. 3. They largely don't write code anymore, agents write ~100% of the code. 4. The bottom line of the companies that employs these engineers and agents (i.e. the terminal purpose of all this code) is typically not budging as a result of AI adoption. This is why you have to think in terms of systems. Automating one aspect of a system creates its own friction and moves the bottlenecks elsewhere.
idees.decryptage: L'"ingénierie logicielle" est le domaine qui consiste à concevoir, développer, tester et maintenir des logiciels. Un "goulot d'étranglement" est un point faible ou une étape lente dans un processus qui limite la performance globale.

    *   Les mathématiciens : "Publiez-le, on s'en fiche désormais."
    *   Les informaticiens : "Mettez-le en open source, mais payez aussi notre conférence."
    *   Les physiciens : "Laissez-nous faire, petits génies."

Il applique déjà ce concept à sa propre entreprise, qu'il appelle une "entreprise auto-pilotée", avec l'objectif qu'elle finisse par fonctionner de manière autonome.

outils.decryptage: Les "traces" d'un modèle d'IA sont des enregistrements détaillés de son fonctionnement interne lorsqu'il traite une information, permettant de comprendre comment il arrive à ses réponses. Les "modèles à poids ouverts" (open-weight models) sont des modèles d'IA dont les paramètres internes (les "poids") sont rendus publics, ce qui permet à quiconque de les utiliser, les étudier et les améliorer. Les "tokens" sont les unités de texte (mots, parties de mots, ponctuations) que le modèle utilise pour traiter et générer du langage.
